text: The Global Positioning System (GPS) is a satellite-based hyperbolic navigation system owned by the United States Space Force and operated by Mission Delta 31. It is one of the global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) that provide geolocation and time information to a GPS receiver anywhere on or near the Earth where signal quality permits. The system does not require users to transmit data and operates independently of telephone or Internet reception, though these technologies can enhance the usefulness of GPS positioning. It provides critical positioning capabilities to military, civil, and commercial users worldwide. Although the U.S. government created, controls, and maintains GPS, it is freely accessible to anyone with a GPS receiver. The GPS project began in 1973 with the U.S. Department of Defense to overcome limitations of earlier navigation systems, combining ideas from predecessors such as LORAN, Decca Navigator, TRANSIT, Timation, and SECOR. Roger L. Easton, Ivan A. Getting, and Bradford Parkinson are credited with inventing GPS, and Gladys West's work on the mathematical geodetic Earth model was instrumental in enabling precise satellite position detection. The system's design incorporates corrections for relativistic effects: GPS satellite clocks run 38 microseconds faster per day than Earth-based clocks, and without correction, position errors would accumulate at up to 10 kilometers per day. The concept originated in 1963 with Project 57 and was further developed in Project 621B, which included many attributes seen in modern GPS. Early navigation systems like TRANSIT (first tested in 1960) and Timation (first launched in 1967) laid foundational technologies, including accurate atomic clocks in space. The U.S. Navy's TRANSIT system provided updates too slowly for Air Force needs, while the Army's SECOR system used ground transmitters and a satellite to determine a user's location. A team led by Harold L. Jury used real-time data assimilation to reduce orbital position errors. In 1973, a meeting at the Pentagon led to the creation of the Defense Navigation Satellite System (DNSS), later named Navstar, with the full constellation designated Navstar-GPS. Ten Block I prototype satellites were launched between 1978 and 1985, with one launch failure. The Air Force Geophysical Research Lab developed the Klobuchar model for ionospheric corrections, with contributions from Elizabeth Essex-Cohen. After the 1980s, civilian use of GPS was limited by Selective Availability (SA), a deliberate error introduced into the signal to degrade civilian accuracy to about 100 meters, which military receivers could correct. Following the Korean Air Lines Flight 007 incident in 1988, President Ronald Reagan directed that GPS be made available for civilian use. During the Gulf War, the temporary disabling of SA occurred due to a shortage of military GPS units, as many U.S. soldiers used civilian receivers. Differential GPS systems from the U.S. Coast Guard, Federal Aviation Administration, and other countries began broadcasting local corrections in the 1990s, reducing both SA and atmospheric effects. The U.S. military also developed local GPS jamming, reducing the need for global degradation. On May 1, 2000, President Bill Clinton signed a directive to disable Selective Availability, providing civilians with the same accuracy as military users, a change proposed by Secretary of Defense William Perry in response to the growth of differential GPS services and military advancements in denial technologies. Selective Availability was removed from the GPS architecture beginning with GPS-III. After its discontinuation, GPS accuracy improved to about 5 meters (16 ft), with L5-band receivers achieving 30 centimeters (12 in) accuracy and high-end applications reaching within 2 cm (3/4 in), even sub-millimeter accuracy with long-term measurements. Consumer devices like smartphones can achieve 4.9 meters (16 ft) or better with assistive services such as Wi-Fi positioning. As of July 2023, 18 GPS satellites broadcast L5 signals, considered pre-operational, with a full complement of 24 expected by 2027. The U.S. Department of Defense is required by law to maintain a continuous, worldwide Standard Positioning Service and to prevent hostile use of GPS without unduly disrupting civilian applications. The Interagency GPS Executive Board (IGEB) oversaw GPS policy from 1996 to 2004, after which the National Space-Based Positioning, Navigation and Timing Executive Committee was established in 2004 to advise federal agencies, chaired jointly by the Deputy Secretaries of Defense and Transportation, with members from State, Commerce, Homeland Security, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and NASA. The GPS satellites carry very stable atomic clocks synchronized with ground control stations, and any clock drift is corrected regularly. Each satellite broadcasts a signal containing its position and time, and a receiver calculates its four-dimensional position in spacetime using data from at least four satellites, solving for three spatial coordinates and its own clock deviation. The receiver measures the time of arrival (TOA) of signals from four satellites, computes pseudo-ranges based on the time of transmission (TOT), and determines its position and clock offset. The system's development was recognized with numerous awards, including the 1992 Robert J. Collier Trophy, the 2003 Charles Stark Draper Prize, the 2011 IAF Global Positioning System 60th Anniversary Award, and the 2018 induction of Gladys West into the Air Force Space and Missile Pioneers Hall of Fame. In 2019, four founding members of the project received the Queen Elizabeth Prize for Engineering. USA-203 from the Block IIR-M series is currently unhealthy. The GPS program cost, including satellite launches but not user equipment, was estimated at US$5 billion (equivalent to $11 billion in 2024) by 1994. Modernization efforts, including the next generation of GPS Block III satellites and the Next Generation Operational Control System (OCX), were authorized by the U.S. Congress in 2000. As of early 2015, high-quality Standard Positioning Service (SPS) receivers provided horizontal accuracy better than 3.5 meters (11 ft).

The signal transmitted by a GPS satellite and received by a ground station is proportional to the distance between them; using distance data from multiple ground stations, the precise location coordinates of a satellite at any given time can be determined. Each GPS satellite carries an accurate record of its own position and time and continuously broadcasts this data. A GPS receiver calculates its four-dimensional position in spacetime—three spatial coordinates and a clock deviation—by receiving signals from at least four satellites, as it must solve for four unknowns. The receiver measures the time of arrival (TOA) of signals according to its own clock, computes time of flight (TOF) values from the TOAs and time of transmission (TOT), and derives pseudo-ranges—ranges plus the time difference between the receiver and satellite clocks multiplied by the speed of light—using the speed of light. These pseudo-ranges are then used to compute the receiver’s three-dimensional position and clock offset, which are solved simultaneously using navigation equations. The resulting Earth-centered position is typically converted to latitude, longitude, and height relative to an ellipsoidal Earth model, and the height may be further adjusted to mean sea level (geoid). As of 2025, GPS modernization through GPS III and GPS IIIF satellites enhances performance with more accurate atomic clocks and stronger, secure, interoperable signals (L1C, L2C, L5), improving time-of-flight measurement precision and resistance to interference. Conceptually, time differences of arrival (TDOAs) define a hyperboloid geometry, with the receiver located at the intersection of three such hyperboloids; however, it is a misconception that three spheres define the user location—this only holds if the receiver’s clock is synchronized with satellite clocks, which would allow three satellites to determine position. In practice, a tracker algorithm improves position and time accuracy, rejects erroneous measurements, and estimates velocity, though velocity changes are delayed and inaccurate at short distances. GPS requires four or more satellites for accurate navigation, but fewer can suffice if one variable—such as altitude—is known (e.g., a ship at near-zero elevation or an aircraft with known height), and receivers may use dead reckoning, inertial navigation, or vehicle data to provide degraded position when fewer than four satellites are visible. The GPS system consists of three segments: space (24 to 32 satellites in medium Earth orbit, with six orbital planes at approximately 55° inclination and 60° separation, orbiting every 11 hours 58 minutes at about 20,200 km altitude), control (managed by the U.S. Space Force via monitoring stations in Hawaii, Kwajalein, Ascension, Diego Garcia, Colorado Springs, and Cape Canaveral, with data processed at Schriever Space Force Base by the 2nd Space Operations Squadron), and user segments (including military and civilian users). As of February 2019, there were 31 satellites in the constellation, with 27 in use and four as spares; a 32nd was launched in 2018 but remained in evaluation. The constellation now has nine satellites typically visible from any point on Earth with a clear horizon, improving redundancy. The control segment uses a Kalman filter to synchronize satellite atomic clocks and update ephemeris data, with the operation control segment (OCS) serving as the current control system until the Next Generation GPS Operation Control System (OCX) is fully operational. OCX, which began development in 2011 and faced delays, was expected to launch in 2021 but was pushed to 2024 and officially accepted by the U.S. Space Force on July 1, 2025, over 8 years and $4 billion behind schedule; OCX Block 3F is being developed to support GPS IIIF satellites, scheduled to launch in 2027. The user segment includes hundreds of thousands of military and tens of millions of civilian and commercial users, with receivers typically containing an antenna, processor, and stable clock. Many receivers support differential corrections via RTCM SC-104 (RS-232, 4,800 bps), though internal DGPS receivers often outperform external ones; as of 2006, low-cost units commonly include WAAS receivers. GPS data can be relayed via NMEA 0183 (used by open-source tools like gpsd) or proprietary protocols such as SiRF and MTK, through serial, USB, or Bluetooth connections. Originally a military system, GPS is now widely used in commerce, science, tracking, and surveillance, with its accurate time enabling applications in banking, mobile operations, and power grid control. The U.S. government restricts export of certain GPS receivers capable of operating above 60,000 ft or at speeds over 1,000 kn, classifying them as munitions requiring export licenses—even if used only for civilian purposes—though disabling high-altitude operation exempts them. These restrictions apply only to U.S.-origin units, with a growing trade in non-U.S. GPS components sold as ITAR-free. GPS was first used in combat during the 1991 Persian Gulf War, demonstrating both utility and vulnerability to jamming, which has since grown as adversaries like Russia, China, North Korea, and Iran have deployed jamming to disrupt operations, including the downing of Flight PS752. In the Russo-Ukrainian War, Russian electronic warfare reduced the effectiveness of GPS-guided munitions from 70% to 6%. Satellite atomic clocks operate on GPS time, which is not adjusted for leap seconds and is 18 seconds ahead of UTC as of January 2017 (due to a leap second added in December 2016), with receivers subtracting this offset to compute UTC. The GPS navigation message includes the GPS-UTC offset, which can accommodate up to 255 leap seconds.

While most clocks derive their time from Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), the atomic clocks on GPS satellites are set to GPS time, which is not adjusted for Earth's rotation and thus does not include leap seconds or other periodic corrections. GPS time was aligned with UTC in 1980 but has since diverged; as of January 2017, GPS time is 18 seconds ahead of UTC due to the leap second added on December 31, 2016. The difference between GPS time and UTC is included in the GPS navigation message, and receivers subtract this offset to compute UTC and specific time zone values. New GPS units may not display correct UTC until they receive the UTC offset message, and the GPS-UTC offset field can accommodate up to 255 leap seconds (eight bits). GPS time is theoretically accurate to about 14 nanoseconds due to clock drift relative to International Atomic Time (TAI), with TAI – GPS equaling 19 seconds, though most receivers are only accurate to about 100 nanoseconds due to signal interpretation errors. GPS applies two major relativistic corrections: one for the relative velocity between satellite and receiver (special relativity) and one for the difference in gravitational potential (general relativity); satellite acceleration is typically not separately corrected. GPS date is expressed as a week number and seconds into the week, with the week number transmitted as a ten-bit field in the C/A and P(Y) navigation messages, resetting every 1,024 weeks (19.6 years). GPS week zero began at 00:00:00 UTC (00:00:19 TAI) on January 6, 1980, and the week number returned to zero on August 21, 1999 and again on April 6, 2019. To determine the current Gregorian date, a receiver must have an approximate date within 3,584 days. The modernized GPS civil navigation (CNAV) message will use a 13-bit field that repeats every 8,192 weeks (157 years), lasting until 2137. GPS satellites broadcast navigation messages on L1 (1.57542 GHz) and L2 (1.2276 GHz) frequencies at 50 bits per second, with each complete message taking 750 seconds (12.5 minutes) and consisting of a 1500-bit frame divided into five 300-bit subframes, each 6 seconds long. Subframes 4 and 5 are subcommutated 25 times, resulting in a total message length of 37,500 bits. The first subframe contains the week number, time within the week, and satellite health; subframes 2 and 3 contain ephemeris data (precise orbital parameters), while subframes 4 and 5 contain almanac data (coarse orbit and status for up to 32 satellites and error correction). Receivers must demodulate signals from each satellite for 18 to 30 seconds to obtain ephemeris data and up to 732 to 750 seconds (12.5 minutes) to collect all almanacs. All satellites use code-division multiple access (CDMA) with unique pseudo-random (PRN) codes: the coarse/acquisition (C/A) code, accessible to the public, transmits at 1.023 million chips per second, and the precise (P/Y) code, encrypted for military use, transmits at 10.23 million chips per second. The satellites' internal clocks operate at 10.22999999543 MHz to compensate for relativistic effects. The L1 carrier is modulated by both C/A and P/Y codes, while L2 is modulated only by the P/Y code. The P/Y code can be encrypted for military access. The L3 signal (1.38105 GHz) is used by the U.S. Nuclear Detonation Detection System (USNDS) to detect and report nuclear detonations, and the L4 band (1.379913 GHz) is being studied for ionospheric correction. The L5 frequency (1.17645 GHz), added during GPS modernization, was first provided by a Block IIF satellite launched in May 2010 and completed with the 12th and final Block IIF satellite launched on February 5, 2016; it consists of two phase-quadrature carriers, each bi-phase shift key (BPSK) modulated, and supports safety-of-life aviation applications. In 2011, LightSquared sought a conditional waiver to operate a terrestrial broadband service near the L1 band, raising concerns about interference with GPS signals, especially in the upper 10 MHz of its spectrum, with testing in early 2011 showing minimal effects in the lower 10 MHz (less than 1% of GPS devices affected) and some concern in the upper range, with Aviation Week reporting "significant jamming" in June 2011. Signals are separated by unique Gold codes assigned to each satellite, and receivers identify satellites by their distinct C/A code patterns. If almanac data is already stored, the receiver selects satellites by their PRNs (1 to 32); otherwise, it enters a search mode until a lock is obtained, requiring an unobstructed line of sight. A delay of up to 30 seconds may occur before the first position estimate due to ephemeris data reading. The receiver uses satellite messages to determine satellite positions and transmission times. The satellite position and time are designated as [xi, yi, zi, si], and the true reception time is ti = t~i − b, where b is the receiver's clock bias relative to the more accurate satellite clocks. The message transit time is t~i − b − si, and the distance traveled is (t~i − b − si)c. With n satellites, the equations are solved for the receiver position [x, y, z] and clock bias b, requiring at least four satellites. The pseudoranges pi = (t~i − si)c are biased versions of true ranges, and the system has four unknowns, requiring at least four signals. When more than four satellites are available, the system is overdetermined and a fitting method is used. Position errors vary with satellite sky configuration, and receivers calculate error estimates using geometric dilution of position (GDOP) factors. The receiver position is typically expressed in WGS 84 coordinates or a country-specific system. The solution can be interpreted as the center of an inscribed sphere of radius bc, touching spheres centered at satellites with radii equal to pseudoranges. The measured pseudoranges contain clock errors, and in idealized cases, the true ranges represent the radii of spheres centered on satellites, with the receiver at their intersection via trilateration. However, in practice, random errors and precision loss from subtracting close numbers reduce accuracy, and three satellites alone are insufficient. More satellites improve accuracy by reducing random errors and increasing sphere separation, though multiple intersections occur, and a best-fit solution is computed via least squares. Subtracting pseudoranges from different satellites cancels the clock bias, resulting in a difference of distances di − dj, which defines a hyperbola in 2D or a hyperboloid in 3D, allowing the receiver to be located at the intersection of three hyperboloids from four satellites. With more satellites, multiple intersections exist, and a best-fitting solution is used. The receiver position and clock bias are solved simultaneously in a four-dimensional spacetime, with each signal describing a hypercone centered on a satellite. When more than four satellites are available, the system uses the best signals or all visible ones, depending on receiver channels, processing power, and GDOP.

The clock in a GPS receiver is typically less accurate than that of the satellites and is not precisely synchronized with them, leading to pseudoranges that differ significantly from true distances. To address this, the time difference between the receiver and satellite clocks is modeled as an unknown bias, denoted as b, and the system of equations is solved simultaneously for the receiver’s position [x, y, z] and the clock bias b. This solution space is viewed as a four-dimensional spacetime, requiring signals from at least four satellites, each of which defines a hypercone (or spherical cone) with its vertex at the satellite and a spherical base; the receiver’s position lies at the intersection of four or more such hypercones. When more than four satellites are available, the system becomes over-determined and solved using least-squares or weighted least-squares methods, as no unique solution exists. These equations are non-linear and typically require iterative methods like the Gauss–Newton algorithm for resolution. Initially, GPS was designed with a numerical least-squares approach before closed-form solutions were developed. One such closed-form solution, by S. Bancroft, is well-documented and claimed to perform better in low-geometric dilution of precision (GDOP) scenarios compared to iterative methods. Bancroft’s method is algebraic and applicable to four or more satellites; with four satellites, it involves inverting a 4x4 matrix and solving a single-variable quadratic equation, yielding one or two solutions, of which only one is typically a near-Earth, physically meaningful solution. For more than four satellites, Bancroft uses the generalized inverse (pseudoinverse). While some argue that iterative methods generally provide more accurate results, Leick et al. (2015) state that Bancroft’s (1985) solution is one of the earliest, if not the first, closed-form solution, with later closed-form solutions published but unclear adoption in practice. GPS error analysis identifies residual errors from sources such as signal arrival time, atmospheric delays (ionospheric and tropospheric), ephemeris and clock data, multipath, and interference, with error magnitude influenced by GDOP. Artificial errors, including jamming and selective availability—which previously limited accuracy to approximately 6–12 meters (20–40 feet) and was discontinued on May 1, 2000—remain a concern. GNSS enhancement techniques improve positioning accuracy by integrating external data, such as error corrections or direct measurements of signal deviations, into the calculation. In the U.S., GPS receivers are regulated under FCC Part 15 rules, which require them to accept interference and to reasonably discriminate against signals outside their allocated spectrum. GPS operates in the 1559 to 1610 MHz band, while LightSquared’s Mobile Satellite Service (MSS) band is 1525 to 1559 MHz. Since 1996, the FCC has authorized use of the adjacent spectrum for LightSquared. In 2001, LightSquared’s predecessor applied for an integrated satellite-terrestrial service; in 2002, the U.S. GPS Industry Council agreed to an out-of-band-emissions (OOBE) agreement to prevent ground-based transmissions from interfering with the GPS band. In 2004, the FCC adopted this agreement, authorizing LightSquared’s Ancillary Tower Components (ATCs) as ancillary to the satellite service, not as a standalone offering. This authorization was reviewed by the U.S. Interdepartment Radio Advisory Committee. In January 2011, the FCC conditionally authorized LightSquared’s wholesale customers—such as Best Buy, Sharp, and C Spire—to resell integrated services using only the 1525 to 1559 MHz band, contingent on interference studies led by LightSquared with GPS industry and federal agency participation. On February 14, 2012, the FCC vacated the conditional order after the NTIA concluded there was no practical way to mitigate GPS interference. GPS receivers are designed to operate beyond the GPS band, up to 400 MHz in either direction of 1575.42 MHz, due to mobile satellite services broadcasting at similar power levels. As per FCC Part 15, GPS receivers are not protected from out-of-band signals, explaining the coexistence of both bands. In 2003, the FCC allowed MSS licensees to build small ancillary ground towers to promote efficient terrestrial spectrum use, noting that the services are imperfect substitutes and operate in different market segments. In 2004, the FCC reiterated that the ground towers remain ancillary. In 2010, the FCC stated LightSquared would offer mobile broadband services to enhance competition, but GPS manufacturers argue this contradicts the 2003 and 2004 rulings that the ATC is ancillary. To support public interest, Trimble Navigation Ltd. formed the "Coalition To Save Our GPS." Both the FCC and LightSquared committed to resolving GPS interference before operation. Aviation experts warn that interference could cause aircraft to go off course undetected, affecting air traffic control, defense guidance, and emergency services like 911. On February 14, 2012, the FCC barred LightSquared’s national broadband network due to the NTIA’s finding that interference could not be mitigated, a decision LightSquared is challenging. Following the U.S. deployment of GPS, other nations have developed their own satellite navigation systems. In the event of space weather or anti-satellite attacks, the U.S. lacks a terrestrial backup; the LORAN-C system was shut down in North America in 2010 and Europe in 2015. eLoran is proposed as a U.S. terrestrial backup but has not received approval or funding as of 2024. China continues to operate LORAN-C transmitters, and Russia has a similar system called CHAYKA ("Seagull").
